title: Just sitting
hook: a cushion, a wall, and no technique at all: Zen's sitting practice

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on contemplative science. Your line was solid and light: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly. What did you keep? Today a new block opens, the world's schools of practice, starting with Zen. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

A round cushion on the floor. A plain wall a few feet away. Someone sits down, crosses their legs, rests their hands in their lap, and then nothing else happens. No counting the breath. No phrase to repeat. No candle, no picture to hold in the mind. For a stretch of time, a person just sits there, awake. That can sound like waiting for the real thing to start. In one Zen school, this is the real thing. The Japanese teacher Dogen gave it a name that sounds almost too plain to be a teaching: just sitting. Today's word is the sitting itself.
screen: `A CUSHION. A WALL.` → `NO TECHNIQUE AT ALL.` → `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: Zazen is the word Zen uses for seated meditation. Dogen's own name for the way he taught it was shikantaza, usually put into English as just sitting. Here's what that looks like. First, it has no technique. Over the last block we met practices with a job to do: count the breath, note the thought, scan the body. Just sitting sets the jobs down. Second, the body does the work. In his short guide to zazen, Dogen's instructions are physical and plain: sit on a cushion, cross the legs, fold the hands, keep the back upright, don't lean left or right, forward or back. Eyes stay open, resting gently. Breath goes quietly through the nose. Third, thoughts. They will come. Dogen doesn't say to fight them, and he doesn't say to follow them. His advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. Then you're simply sitting again. He passes on an old exchange about this, too: asked what you think about while sitting, a teacher answers, roughly, think of not-thinking. And how do you do that? Non-thinking. It's meant to be a little puzzling. Fourth, and this is the surprising part: for Dogen, sitting isn't a tool for getting enlightenment later. He taught that practice and awakening aren't two separate things. The sitting is already the thing it's looking for. That's a hard idea to hold in your head, which may be why he kept handing people a cushion instead of an argument. Zen has more than one school. The Soto school, which traces itself to Dogen, puts just sitting at the heart of practice. Rinzai Zen also sits zazen, and often adds something else to the cushion. That's tomorrow.
screen: `A SITTING WITH NO TECHNIQUE.` · `BACK UPRIGHT, EYES OPEN, BREATH QUIET.` · `A THOUGHT COMES: NOTICE, AND IT GOES.` · `NOT A TOOL. THE SITTING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: just sit. On a chair is fine. Feet on the floor, back upright but not stiff. Rest your hands in your lap. Let your eyes stay open, gazing softly at the floor or a wall a little ahead. Breathe through your nose and leave the breath alone. When a thought shows up, notice it, and come back to sitting. There's nothing to get right. If you'd like to try a longer sit, ten minutes some other day is a good next step. For now, two. The bell holds the time.
Zazen. Seated meditation in Zen. In Dogen's way of teaching it, just sitting, with nothing added. Today's word.

Your line: just sitting. Today, the next time you sit down somewhere, on a bus, at a desk, in a waiting room, take three breaths of just sitting before you reach for anything. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit zazen as shikantaza, upright with eyes open and no object of focus, often in a meditation hall together and at set times of day.

myth: in just sitting, you close your eyes and count the breath
Dogen's instructions keep the eyes open, and just sitting sets aside techniques like counting.
Dogen's advice about thoughts is to notice them, not fight them or follow them
in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes.
for Dogen, sitting is a tool for getting enlightenment later
he taught that practice and awakening aren't two separate things. the sitting is already it.

fork.setup: you're sitting zazen and a thought about tomorrow's meeting shows up. going by Dogen's advice, what do you do?
options: push it away hard and clear your mind.
notice it, and come back to sitting.
follow it and plan the meeting properly.
fork.reveal: Dogen's advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. no fight, no chase.

original.note: Japanese: the word Zen uses for seated meditation.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means doing something with your mind.
what it means: zazen, in Dogen's way, is just sitting: upright, eyes open, no technique, letting thoughts come and go.
what a scholar hears: shikantaza, and Dogen's teaching that practice and awakening are one, so the sitting isn't a means to an end.

sources.ref: Bendowa (on the oneness of practice and awakening)

notes: Editor pass: varied the repeated 'turned four ways' teach frame; changed 'to a lot of us' to avoid speaking for the listener.

Posture instructions (cushion, crossed legs, folded hands, upright, not leaning, eyes open, quiet breath through the nose) are paraphrased from Fukanzazengi; confirm the details, especially 'through the nose'.

The thought advice ('when a thought arises, notice it; in the noticing it goes') and the 'think of not-thinking ... non-thinking' exchange (attributed to Yaoshan, passed on by Dogen) are paraphrased; confirm attribution and wording.
The oneness of practice and awakening (shusho itto) is drawn from Bendowa; confirm the plain-language summary.
Soto/Rinzai framing: Soto traces itself to Dogen and centers shikantaza; Rinzai also sits zazen and often adds koans. Confirm fairness.
The outline's '13th-century Japan' was left out under the claims rule. The outline practice is ten minutes; the app sit is two, so ten minutes is offered as an optional next step.
